title: Perfect squares and difference of two squares
log: 2026-11-04T09:36:56Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The bank card teaches the same two identities, but as part of a broader factorising card that also covers common factors and grouping, and it is pitched at Victorian Units 1 and 2 rather than Year 9 expansion, so it is not a close enough match to reuse or adapt.

draft.title: Perfect squares and difference of two squares
card: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Square the first term, double the product of the two terms, then square the last term.
Worked example: (x + 4)² = x² + 2 × x × 4 + 4² = x² + 8x + 16. Note that (x + 4)² is not x² + 16.
(a + b)(a − b) = a² − b². The middle terms cancel, so only two terms are left.
Worked example: (x + 5)(x − 5) = x² − 25. The brackets must have the same two terms, one with + and one with −.
draft.remember: A squared bracket has a middle term 2ab. Matching brackets with + and − have no middle term.

a.why: Using (a + b)², the middle term is 2 × x × 6 = 12x and the last is 6² = 36. The answer x² + 36 is tempting, but it leaves out the middle term.
a.clue: Double the product of x and 6 for the middle term.

b.why: The brackets match except for the sign, so the middle terms cancel and the answer is y² − 9² = y² − 81. Writing y² + 81 mixes this up with a perfect square, which has a plus sign for the last term.
b.clue: The y terms with 9 cancel out.
